body: {"total":7,"records":[{"title":"Chasing signatures: a qualitative study of residents' experiences of entrustable professional activity assessment","authors":"Okafor-Lindgren T, Brennan-Mwale S, Castillo-Hart R","year":2022,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Journal of Clinical Education","doi":"10.5555/kjce.2022.0187","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Background: competency-based residency programmes require residents to collect workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities, but little is known about how residents experience the workload. Methods: we conducted semi-structured interviews with 24 residents in three internal medicine programmes and analysed the transcripts with reflexive thematic analysis. Results: residents described spending time chasing assessors at the end of rotations, choosing straightforward activities that supervisors were likely to observe, and treating the assessment target as an administrative quota. Several residents said they had stopped asking for assessments after difficult encounters because they feared a low rating would follow them. Conclusions: residents experienced assessment as a burden to be managed strategically; programmes should examine whether numerical targets undermine the formative purpose of assessment."},{"title":"Assessors' accounts of entrustment decisions and narrative comments under clinical time pressure","authors":"Varga-Nwosu E, Holmberg-Achebe L","year":2020,"venue":"Vellmar Review of Workplace Assessment","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held focus groups with 31 faculty assessors in two academic hospitals to explore how they complete workplace-based assessments of entrustable professional activities. Assessors reported completing forms in batches, often days after the observed activity, and relying on memory of the resident rather than of the specific encounter. Many described writing brief narrative comments because they believed the comments were rarely read by anyone. Assessors valued a short conversation with the resident more than the form itself, and several said the form had replaced the conversation. The authors suggest that assessment design should reduce documentation time and make the feedback conversation, not the form, the unit of assessment."},{"title":"Timeliness and narrative length of entrustable professional activity assessments: an analysis of mobile application records","authors":"Mensah-Kowalski D, Fairbairn-Osei J, Tanaka-Ruiz P","year":2024,"venue":"Kestrelmoor Journal of Clinical Education","doi":"10.5555/kjce.2024.0033","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We analysed 41,206 completed assessments of entrustable professional activities from a mobile assessment application used by 11 residency programmes over two academic years. The median delay between the observed activity and completion of the form was two days, and 29 percent of assessments were completed more than seven days later. Narrative comments on assessments completed after seven days were shorter (median 11 words) than comments on assessments completed on the same day (median 24 words). Entrustment ratings rose steadily through the year whatever the delay. Delay was greatest in the final week of each rotation. Timeliness may be a useful process marker of assessment quality, but these data cannot show why assessors delay."},{"title":"Assessment burden in competency-based postgraduate medical education: a scoping review","authors":"Delacroix-Mbeki A, Sorensen-Adeyemi F, Kaur-Whitfield N, Brandt-Oduya T","year":2021,"venue":"Harthill Health Professions Education Reports","doi":"10.5555/hhper.2021.0412","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We mapped how assessment burden has been defined and studied in competency-based postgraduate training. We searched four bibliographic databases and included 46 reports published to 2020. Burden was most often described as time spent completing forms, but reports also described cognitive and emotional burden for residents and assessors and administrative burden for programmes. Only nine reports collected primary data from both residents and assessors, and none examined how burden changed after programmes altered their assessment targets. We found no agreed definition or measure of assessment burden. We recommend studies that include residents, assessors and programme administrators together and that describe the assessment system in enough detail for comparison."},{"title":"Program directors' views on minimum numbers of workplace-based assessments per rotation: a national survey","authors":"Rutherford-Kimani B, Esposito-Lund H","year":2019,"venue":"Cindervale Postgraduate Training Letters","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We surveyed programme directors of internal medicine and family medicine residencies about the minimum number of workplace-based assessments they required per four-week rotation. Of 212 directors invited, 131 responded (62 percent). The median required number was 10 (range 4 to 20). Directors who set higher targets were more likely to report late or incomplete assessments, and 58 percent said that their targets had been chosen without evidence. Most directors wanted guidance on how many assessments are needed for a defensible competency decision. Responding directors may differ from those who did not respond, and the survey did not ask residents or assessors about their experience."},{"title":"Tick-box culture: chief residents' perspectives on the purpose of competency assessment","authors":"Achterberg-Silva M, Nakamura-Obi K","year":2017,"venue":"Vellmar Review of Workplace Assessment","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Chief residents occupy a middle position between residents and faculty in assessment systems. We conducted three focus groups with 17 chief residents from five programmes. Participants described a tick-box culture in which the number of completed forms signalled engagement rather than learning. They reported that residents who were struggling were the least likely to request assessments, so the programme noticed their difficulties late. Chief residents proposed fewer and better assessments linked to direct observation and a regular coaching conversation. The study predates the full introduction of entrustable professional activities in the participating programmes, and the chief residents were selected by their programme directors."},{"title":"Reducing required assessments from twelve to eight per rotation: effect on narrative comment quality in one residency programme","authors":"Fitzgerald-Onu C, Park-Hallstrom I, Moreau-Ansah G","year":2025,"venue":"Harthill Health Professions Education Reports","doi":"10.5555/hhper.2025.0098","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"One internal medicine programme reduced its minimum number of entrustable professional activity assessments from twelve to eight per four-week rotation. We compared assessments from the year before and the year after the change. Two raters blinded to the period scored 600 sampled narrative comments with a structured quality rubric. The proportion of comments rated as specific and actionable rose from 34 percent to 47 percent, and the median comment length increased from 12 to 19 words. The total number of assessments fell by 28 percent. Progression decisions made by the competency committee were unchanged. The comparison is uncontrolled, and faculty development sessions on feedback were also introduced in the same year."}]}
